newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Bahamas incumbent PM is former protege of rival.
newsitem.headline: Bahamas incumbent PM is former protege of rival.

text.p: Hubert Ingraham, who easily won a second term as Bahamas prime minister with his party's victory in Friday's general election, is a man of humble origins who set out to reform both the country's economy and the tainted image of its politics.

In his first term he lured big international investors to his archipelago nation. He also tried to shed the veneer of corruption surrounding politicians and clean up the 500-island chain's reputation as a drug-smuggling staging post.

He embarked on a program of privatization and voters responded to his efforts by awarding him a second term through his Free National Movement's (FNM) victory over the PLP. By late Friday, election officials said the FNM would take at least 33 out of the 40 seats in the nation's parliament.

Ingraham is the former protege of PLP leader Sir Lynden Pidling, the dominant figure in Bahamian politics through the advent of black majority rule, independence from Britain and up to Ingraham's sweeping victory in 1992 elections, but one of only a handful of PLP candidates expected to take seats in parliament in Friday's vote.
A big, heavyset man, Ingraham can talk like a stern lawmaker but is also known as a man of the people. Much of the FNM's success is attributed to his energy and vision.

After taking office in 1992, his administration renovated dilapidated schools, public buildings and docks, privatized money-draining hotels and attracted major new investment including names like Sun International, Disney and Hutchison International Port Holdings, a subsidiary of Hutchison Whampoa Ltd of Hong Kong.
He pledged his second government would continue on that course and promised employment to all those who want work.

Ingraham entered politics in the PLP but was forced out of the cabinet in 1984. He was expelled from the party in 1986 after demanding more accountability after a drug-trafficking and corruption scandal tainted some Pindling associates.

For the next few years he was not affiliated to a party and won a seat in parliament as an independent in 1987. In April 1990, he joined the opposition FNM and within weeks became its leader and a natural candidate for prime minister.
Although many Bahamians associated the FNM with the old white-dominated United Bahamian Party (UBP) Ingraham, a product of a humble black family, had pro-independence and nationalist credentials.

He was born at Pine Ridge on the island of Grand Bahama on Aug. 4, 1947, and grew up at Cooper's Town on the island of Abaco, where he attended local schools. Later, he earned a high school diploma at night school.
The Bahamas is too small to have a university of its own, and Ingraham, unlike many members of the political elite, never studied abroad.
He was an apprentice with a law firm and in 1972 was admitted to the bar as a practicing attorney. He became a senior partner in one of the Bahamas' most prestigious law firms.
Ingraham entered politics in 1975, rising quickly in the PLP. He was elected to parliament in 1977 and again in 1982 when he became Minister of Housing, National Insurance and Social Services.
He is married to Delores Velma Miller, a schoolteacher. He is the father of six children.
